name: Hydroxytyrosol

lead: Hydroxytyrosol is a phenolic compound found in olives, olive leaves and olive oil, formed from oleuropein in the fruit. It is sold as a supplement and used as an antioxidant ingredient in cosmetics.

The appearance angle is skin care: antioxidant and anti-inflammatory polyphenols are marketed for protecting skin from oxidative stress. Human trials concern markers such as blood-lipid oxidation, inflammation and cardiovascular risk rather than skin appearance.

paras: People consume it through olive oil and olive-leaf or olive-fruit extracts, and it appears as an ingredient in topical products. Products vary in strength.

EFSA considers it safe as a novel food at a no-observed-adverse-effect level of 50 mg/kg body weight per day, and the US treats it as generally recognized as safe in processed foods at up to 5 mg per serving. As a pure chemical it is classified as a skin and eye irritant [1].

angle.text: Used in supplements and topicals as an antioxidant for skin and general health. Studies measure internal biomarkers rather than skin appearance.

lead: Hydroxytyrosol (C8H10O3) is a phenylethanoid found in olives, olive leaves, olive oil and wine. In the body and in the fruit it is released from oleuropein, and ripe black olives contain much more than green ones [1].

The wiki's interest is appearance: it is an antioxidant used in dietary supplements and in skin-care products aimed at protecting skin from oxidative stress and inflammation. Reviews of olive polyphenols describe antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties [2][3].

The European Food Safety Authority authorized a claim that olive oil polyphenols, including hydroxytyrosol, protect blood lipids from oxidative damage when oil contains at least 5 mg per 20 g [1]. Trials in humans have examined antioxidant and inflammatory markers in people with overweight and prediabetes and platelet function in cardiovascular risk [4][5].
infobox: Olives, olive leaf, olive oil, wine
EFSA: protection of blood lipids from oxidative damage

paras: Hydroxytyrosol arises from oleuropein through the enzyme beta-glucosidase. Canned processed olives contain little because iron salts speed its oxidation [1]. About 98 percent of the hydroxytyrosol in plasma and urine after olive oil is in conjugated forms, with a half-life near 2.4 hours [1].

Reviews describe polyphenols from olive oil as antioxidant and anti-inflammatory [2][3]. A 2025 randomized, placebo-controlled trial in people with overweight and prediabetes reported improved antioxidant and anti-inflammatory status with supplementation [4], and a 2025 randomized trial examined platelet function and treatment response in cardiovascular risk [5]. A bioavailability and toxicity review covers its clinical applications [6].

EFSA treats it as safe as a novel food with a NOAEL of 50 mg/kg body weight per day; the US considers it GRAS in processed foods up to 5 mg per serving. As a pure chemical it irritates skin and eyes [1].
Randomized trials have measured oxidative and inflammatory markers and cardiovascular outcomes [4][5]. No trial in the sources measured skin appearance.
